doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: The Jimmy Knepper tribute project
summary: Knepper's daughter Robin gave Watkins his horns, leading to a sold-out Wheeling tribute concert and a record.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That’s a good answer. So Jimmy Knepper. It’s nice that you paid attention to him like you did because there’s an awful lot of musicians in sort of that middle ground that as time goes by they don’t get the recognition. So that was a very passionate excursion for you.
It was, because how it started. Are you aware how this started?
I read your little interview on line. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

His daughter and my mother, his wife and daughter and my mother went to the same church. My mother still goes there. It’s a Unitarian church. And yeah, so they were friends. My mother was good friends with Jimmy’s wife, whatever. But anyway, time moved on and she passed but Jimmy’s daughter Robin was still there at the church with my mother and my mother — it just kind of came together and my mother, “You know who Jimmy Knepper is?” “Yeah, of course I know Jimmy Knepper.” His daughter goes here she has some mouthpieces for you, she’s wondering if you wanted them. And I reached out to her and kind of didn’t hear back and then my mother circled back a while later and said, “Hey, Robin’s talking about maybe giving you Jimmy’s horn.” So I connected with Robin. Jimmy Knepper died in Wheeling, West Virginia, where I grew up. Because that’s where Robin and her husband were living at the time. So when they had to leave Staten Island because they were getting old, you know, he I think eventually developed Parkinson’s. They cared for them in Wheeling, her mother and Buck. So that’s how this all kind of came together. So when this is a few years ago Robin decided it was time to pass along Jimmy’s physical things — the horn — it meant a lot to her even because she associated so much with him. And she is just this beautiful person. And when I went down there to see her as they’re getting ready to move and they’re getting their place in order and getting it ready to sell. I walk in and there’s like nine trombones and a trumpet and some other things on a bed, and mouthpieces and mutes and all this stuff. She gave me a horn. She gave me several horns. And it was so profound. I shared all this with my good friend and collaborator Matt Parker. He’s a saxophonist from Brooklyn. And so we started working on this tribute concert for Jimmy Knepper and we just went in all the way, Jimmy Knepper, and we realized it was like even more than what we were aware of. Of course we know about the Charles Mingus work, and he’s kind of framed in that world as like a copyist. But then again he’s also, if you dig a little deeper you’ll see that he’s included as one of three of the most important contributors in Mingus’ career. Danny Richmond, Eric Dolphy and Jimmy Knepper. So we went and did this big concert and it was sold out. It was in Wheeling at the Stifel Fine Arts Center, and Robin was there. And it was really, that was all it was. And she, I’m just telling you the emotion, the love and the feeling that is just around her — and I have a daughter so I’m seeing this woman, who is twenty years older than me, I’m seeing her as a little girl. I’m seeing her as my daughter. And so all this experience is touching me on another level. And then after that happened another bass player from Pittsburgh, who executive produces a lot of records, his name is Mark Perna, he showed some interest in supporting us for a record date. So then we were like wow, we’re going to make a record. So then we got to go even further into the Jimmy Knepper legacy. And then we got to share those compositions with the musicians on the date. They were just blown away by the © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

heaviness in Jimmy’s work. So just the whole experience was unbelievable. And I was just caught in the wave you know. I had only known Jimmy — I never had a Jimmy Knepper record, maybe one. I had all the Mingus stuff because I’m a Mingus fanatic so I had all the Mingus stuff but — so it brought me really close to him as an artist.
